flawed_step: Step 2 of the proof attempt. Step 1 was: every line graph is claw-free, and L(G) is k-connected exactly when G is essentially k-edge-connected. That step is justified. Step 2 would need a general way to go from 3-connected plus claw-free to a Hamiltonian cycle. By Harary–Nash-Williams, L(G) has a Hamiltonian cycle only if G has a closed trail that touches every edge. Being essentially 3-edge-connected does not give such a trail. The known version of the theorem needs 4-connectivity (the Matthews–Sumner conjecture), and the 3-connected case has counterexamples. So this step cannot be justified.
counterexample: Start with the Petersen graph P and attach one pendant edge to each of its 10 vertices; call the result G. Let H = L(G), which has 25 vertices. H is claw-free because it is a line graph. H is 3-connected: if an edge cut of G leaves an edge on both sides, then both sides contain Petersen vertices (the pendant leaves alone span no edges). Since P is 3-edge-connected, such a cut has at least 3 edges, so G is essentially 3-edge-connected. H is not Hamiltonian: a Hamiltonian cycle in L(G) would need a closed trail in G touching every edge. To touch every pendant edge, that trail must pass through all 10 Petersen vertices. Every Petersen vertex has degree 3 in P, so the trail cannot repeat a vertex and must be a Hamiltonian cycle of P. P has no Hamiltonian cycle, so H has none either.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. The Matthews–Sumner conjecture asks whether 4-connected claw-free graphs are Hamiltonian; with only 3-connectivity there are counterexamples. One is the line graph of the Petersen graph with a pendant edge attached at every vertex. It is claw-free and 3-connected, but a Hamiltonian cycle in it would give a Hamiltonian cycle of the Petersen graph, which does not exist.
